body_markdown:
If presented with a lineup and asked to select the person who spends weekends going 330 mph, you probably wouldn’t pick Doug Kalitta.


Your eyes would likely settle on his uncle, drag-racing legend Connie Kalitta—burly, bear-like, with his big, crooked grin, and at 88 still keenly aware of how the family’s three drag racing teams are doing. You’d certainly spot Connie’s contemporary and archenemy, “Big Daddy” Don Garlits,[still going strong at 94](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/don-garlits-father-of-swamp-rat-ufo-enthusiast-and-unequivocally-the-greatest-drag-racer-ever/) as he presides over his drag racing museum in Florida.


Though the mild-mannered Doug Kalitta—yes, that’s a cliché, but it genuinely fits—is busy writing his name in the NHRA Top Fuel record books alongside Uncle Connie and Big Daddy, he won’t be remembered for the occasionally outrageous antics of those two pioneers, much of which were captured in the film *Heart Like a Wheel* (1983), the story of how Connie and Big Daddy balked at allowing driver Shirley Muldowney into their exclusive club. Connie was played by Beau Bridges. The casting was appropriate.


Cameron Neveu


No, Doug will likely be remembered for guiding Kalitta Motorsports’ three-car team to the absolute top of the NHRA performance charts, and for helping to resurrect, then expand, his uncle’s global freight-hauling aviation business, Kalitta Air, which Connie founded in 1967 with one twin-engine Cessna 310. His fleet now includes 22 Boeing 747s and 16 777s. Since childhood, Doug has maintained a lifelong pair of passions: flying and racing. Now 62 years old, that hasn’t changed.


Cameron Neveu


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Cameron Neveu


Doug’s talent and astonishing work ethic showed themselves early: At 18, he began working for his uncle Connie’s airline as an apprentice under line service mechanics. At 19, he began flying with Connie to the racetrack on the weekends. There, he was “the bottom-end guy,” responsible for removing, inspecting, and servicing the engine’s oil pan, rods, and crankshaft between runs, a role he filled on the weekends until he was 25. At the same time, he began flying commercially and earned his Airframe and Powerplant License from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), qualifying him to service both an aircraft’s body and its engine.


He advanced to leadership positions even as he continued to repair and fly bigger planes with more complex engines. At 21, he had earned his Learjet license and managed a shop that maintained Honeywell TPE331s, gas-turbine engines that spin propellers for light aircraft. At 24, he progressed to managing a shop that maintained Pratt & Whitney JT3D engines, an older turbofan design in which the turbine spins a fan, rather than a propeller. Variants of the JT3D have powered much larger planes, including Boeing B-52 bombers and Douglas DC-8 narrow-body jetliners.


While he was hoping for a dragster seat to open up, Doug discovered short-oval racing. In 1991 he started racing[four-cylinder “midgets”](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/midget-race-rookie-chili-bowl-2022/) in the United States Auto Club (USAC), the premier sanctioning body for open-wheel racing, promptly earning rookie of the year at age 27. He seems to be one of those people who performs better under higher load: In the mid-‘80s, Connie had bought a company that flew DC-8s, and Doug started a shop to maintain all 100 engines. In 1992, at 28, he became one of the youngest DC-8 pilots. The next year, Doug was promoted at Connie’s company, by then called American International Airways, to Vice President of Central and South American Sales in Miami, Florida. He fulfilled this role while managing and piloting DC-8s, Learjets, and Mitsubishi MU2s, and while racing—and winning in—sprint cars, the gnarlier, V-8-powered relatives of midgets. In ‘94, he won the USAC National Sprint Car Championship.


Connie Kalitta, Bounty Hunter.


Kalitta Motorsports


His reputation as a driver was the polar opposite of his firebrand uncle’s. Doug says Connie lived for “a good old argument or fist fight.” Then, as now, Doug preferred to let his driving do the talking. Tony Stewart, who competed in USAC at the same time as Doug and now competes against him[as a driver and as a team owner in Top Fuel](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/tony-stewart-out-wife-leah-pruett-back-in-the-family-top-fuel-dragster-for-2026/) , describes Doug as “ultra competitive.” He was “always focused,” though not in an intense way, Stewart says; Doug was simply quiet and kept to himself. His specialty was the pavement tracks, like Winchester Speedway, Salem Speedway, and Indianapolis Raceway Park. “Big, fast racetracks are where Doug was absolutely amazing. I mean, the speed didn’t bother him.”


Multidisciplinary race car driver Tony Stewart in his R+L Carriers Top Fuel dragster at the Summit Racing Equipment NHRA Nationals, 2026.


Cameron Neveu


The long-awaited NHRA opportunity appeared in 1998, when Connie’s son Scott, Doug’s cousin, decided to retire from NHRA Top Fuel. By then, Connie was no longer driving a full season. His one-man flight operation had grown into that conglomeration called American International Airways, which was now one of the world’s top 25 largest airlines, with revenues over $400 million. In 1997, Connie sold AIA, and its associated maintenance and logistics companies, to Dallas-based Kitty Hawk, Inc., allowing Connie to start another company, Kalitta Leasing. To supervise the merger, he raced only eight times during his nephew’s debut NHRA season in 1998.


At Doug’s first Top Fuel start, the starting line was crowded, as usual, with people eager to see how the new driver would perform. Even more than in other forms of racing, the biggest threat to a new driver is himself. If you haven’t experienced a Top Fuel launch first-hand, it’s impossible to grasp the violence. There is simply no way to consciously prepare; by the time you’ve registered (and become embarrassed by) your reflexive, whole-body flinch, the physical force of the sound waves has passed through your body as if the sound were a 747 and your body a cloud. The driver must wrangle that fury, 11,000 hp exploding directly behind his head, pointed straight down the narrow lane, and trust his life to his parachutes.


Cameron Neveu


That first race, when Doug’s dragster launched, it pulled the front wheels off the ground. Doug did exactly what the car needed: He “pedaled” it, modulating the throttle to lower the front wheels, settle the car, and keep it straight. “It looked like I knew exactly what I was doing,” he laughs. “It was the dumbest luck.” His run left quite an impression on operations manager and ex-Funny Car driver Chad Head, who grew up at the drag strip with his dad, Jim, an innovative tuner and racer. Doug took to drag racing like it was “second nature,” Chad says. “That just doesn’t happen.”


Like any true competitor, Doug wasn’t simply drag-racing to go fast; he was in it to win. His first national event win came about halfway through his debut season, at the NHRA Autolite Nationals in Sonoma, California. The hunt for his first title took much, much longer. Between ‘98 and 2019, he finished second in points six times, twice at the hands of Tony Schumacher, backed by gifted crew chief Alan Johnson. That relentless commitment, says Top Fuel rival Tony Stewart, defines him. “Doug just grinds it out, whether it’s business, whether it’s racing. Nothing fazes him. If he doesn’t succeed, he’s just going to keep digging ‘till he does.”


Cameron Neveu


As he chased that elusive championship, Doug took on new roles in his professional and in his personal life. The company that had bought Connie’s airline in ’97 went into bankruptcy three years later, ceasing operations and filing Chapter 11 bankruptcy in April 2000. Connie was determined to resurrect his airline. However, he mostly wanted the 121 aircraft certificate, which would allow him to operate scheduled cargo flights with large planes; he wasn’t as interested in running the smaller planes, including the Learjets, down in Ypsilanti, at Willow Run Airport. Would Doug be interested? Yes, he would be.


In 2001, Doug took command of Kalitta Charters, with 11 planes. He shortly acquired Kalitta Turbines and DK Turbines (both repair stations, the former in Ypsilanti, Michigan, the latter in Hollister, California). Two years later, Doug added Kalitta Charters II, an airline that handles scheduled, rather than chartered, passenger operations. Today, the family air freight business is thriving once again: Despite Connie’s insistence that he only wanted to run three 747s, his fleet of “seven-fours” has grown to 22, plus 16 Boeing 777s. Doug, who started with one company, now manages five companies and 60 planes. They’re Kalittas, after all: They don’t do anything halfway.


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


As he took over the charter business, Doug’s family was growing. He and his wife Josie welcomed a son, Mitch, in 2001 and a daughter, Avery, in 2003. Though some wondered if he’d step away from drag racing while his kids were young, Doug stuck with it. He clearly made it work; his kids are both successful adults. After graduating from Northwood University, Mitch took a job in the accounting department of Kalitta Charters, flying to the track with his dad on the weekends. His interest in flying blossomed, as well: This year he earned his twin-engine license and his twin-engine instrument rating, which allows him to fly in situations where he cannot navigate by sight, such as in clouds and during fog or rain. After graduating from the University of Michigan, Avery married her high-school boyfriend and signed a multi-year deal with a women’s soccer team in Louisville, Kentucky. When asked how she feels about all this drag-racing business, Avery shrugs and smiles. It’s just what Dad does on the weekend at this point, as normal as her brother in the pits, cleaning parts or packing her dad’s parachutes.


Mitch, far right, put on earplugs as Doug lowers himself into his Mac Tools dragster.


Cameron Neveu


Drag racing and the Kalitta family have been deeply marked by each other, for the better and for the worse. Connie’s place in the record books is assured. Back in the day, he branded himself “The Bounty Hunter,” writing a list of drivers on the side of his dragster and crossing them off as he beat them. He boasts two championships in the[International Hot Rod Association (IHRA)](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/how-darryl-cuttells-would-be-ihra-empire-came-crashing-down/) , one in ’79 and another in ’82, and 10 NHRA national event wins across a 30-year span. The first Top Fuel driver to hit 200 mph in an NHRA-sanctioned event (in 1964), he is also the first driver in any drag-racing series to hit 290 mph (1989). In 2016, the NHRA honored him with its first Lifetime Achievement award. As a team owner, he’s won five world championships: two with Doug, one with funny car driver J.R. Todd in 2018, one with Del Worsham in 2015, and two in ’94 and ’95 thanks to his late son, Scott.


Scott Kalitta, Connie’s son, in June 2008.


Getty Images/Mike Dinovo/LAT Images


About Scott Kalitta: When we visit the[sparkling clean garages of the Kalitta race shop](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/doug-kalitta-eyes-up-a-third-top-fuel-championship/) in Ypsilanti, Doug leads us down a hallway lined with framed photos, noting some vintage shots of Connie’s car, and pointing out his own first win, in Sonoma. He pauses before a section at the end devoted to Scott. Drag racing ran in his blood, too: He raced funny cars and dragsters and boasted 18 wins and two Top Fuel Funny Car championships. Everything ended on Saturday, June 21, 2008, at Englishtown, New Jersey. During a qualifying run, the engine in Scott’s DHL Toyota Solara Funny Car exploded, swallowing the car in flames and tearing its body partially off the chassis. The parachutes did not release. Scott’s smoking car slid through the shutdown area “at a high rate of speed,” hit and then flipped over a wall, and hit a TV camera boom. He was pronounced dead at the hospital.


Doug did not race Sunday. Neither did Scott’s other teammates, David Grubnic and Hillary Will. As Doug stands in the hallway of the race shop, looking at his cousin’s picture, the memory makes him fall quiet, mid-sentence. “That was an unfortunate day.”


Scott Kalitta in his DHL Toyota Solara Funny Car, 2008.


Corbis/Icon Sportswire via Getty


Scott’s death reshaped the sport he loved: Beginning on July 11, 2008, NHRA shortened tracks from a quarter-mile (1320 feet) to 1000 feet for its fastest classes, the nitro-burning Top Fuel and Funny Cars. Over the next two years, it developed and mandated a system for those two classes that automatically shuts off fuel and ignition and deploys the parachutes when a car passes the finish line, if the driver hasn’t already done so. The Kalitta team continues to pay honor to Scott: Doug’s marketing manager, Luke Fath, who grew up next door to Scott Kalitta in Florida and is very close with his sons Corey and Colin, found a panel off the side of one of Scott’s dragsters in southeast Michigan on Facebook Marketplace. It now decorates the bar in the basement of his house on Belleville Lake, across the water from Connie’s place.


Crew chief and tuning wizard Alan Johnson.


Andy Cross/Denver Post via Getty Images


Doug’s NHRA fortunes began to shift in 2022, when renowned crew chief Alan Johnson joined his team. It was a major turning of the tide: “I’ve always liked Doug,” says Johnson, “but we’ve also beat up on him pretty good throughout the years.” Alan brought his long-time assistant crew chief, Brian Husen, who took on the lead role of tuning the other Kalitta dragster, driven by 35-time event winner Shawn Langdon.


Alan Johnson changed “pretty much everything, top to bottom,” switching both Kalitta dragsters over to clutches and flywheels, superchargers, and clutch management[of his own design](https://www.alanjohnsonperformance.com/) . The scope of the changes wasn’t a surprise to Doug or to Shawn: “If you want to set track records and you want to run big speed and you want to win races, all this stuff has got to change,” Alan told them. Doug’s team struggled in 2022 and in the first part of the 2023 season, but, as Alan expected, he and Brian were “the one last element” that Doug needed. In 2023, at the In-N-Out Burger NHRA Finals, Doug defeated Leah Pruett in the final round to become the 2023 Top Fuel world champion.


MediaNews Group via Getty Images


MediaNews Group via Getty Images


MediaNews Group via Getty Images


“Nobody knows what his frustration was behind closed doors the years that he didn’t win,” says Tony Stewart. “But even when he did win, the celebration wasn’t like, ‘Oh my gosh, after all these years’—it just was a normal Doug. He’s just smiling and happy and thanking everybody, and that was it.”


Alan Johnson, working his magic on Doug’s Mac Tool dragster during the Summit Racing Equipment NHRA Nationals.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Kalitta Motorsports was a powerhouse already, and Alan Johnson took it to a new level. After coming second in points to four-time Top Fuel champ Antron Brown in 2024, Doug won his second NHRA championship in 2025. His teammate, Shawn Langdon, was runner-up. This year, Doug was the first Top Fuel driver to capture two event wins. He and his Mac Tools dragster set a track record at zMax Dragway in April of 2026 (3.692 seconds at 342.98 mph), the third-fastest run in NHRA history. In May of 2026, teammate Shawn Langdon made the fastest pass ever in the NHRA, hitting 345 mph. Headed into the six-race Countdown to the Championship playoffs, which kick off this weekend with the Dodge NHRA Great Lakes Nationals at Martin, Michigan, the two are neck-and-neck, separated by only 26 points, with Doug in first.


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


To be a successful team means cultivating relationships with its sponsors, and Kalitta Motorsports is very good at it. The team may no longer have manufacturer support from Toyota, but their win record shows it hasn’t slowed them down. (Toyota also let them keep the funny car bodies after the brand pulled out of drag racing[after the 2025 season](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/toyota-announces-its-leaving-the-nhra-after-2025/) .) The atmosphere at 1 Woodward Avenue in downtown Detroit during Kalitta’s annual partner summit is one of easy camaraderie between the team and the sponsors, some of whom are in very long relationships with Kalitta. DHL, a flight partner of Kalitta Air, has sponsored the race team for 20 years. Fifth Third, a partner for eight years, has just re-signed for four more. Mac Tools and Kalitta represent one of the longest partnerships in the NHRA. Kalitta embraces events like these with pride, says general manager Chad Head, the same reason that at each of the 20-plus events on the NHRA schedule, Kalitta brings an extra, 53-foot trailer exclusively for hospitality, staffed by three people who are paid full-time.


Connie isn’t in attendance due to a knee injury at Sonoma, but you can feel his presence in the room. Doug, wearing his red-and-white Mac Tools polo and a pair of square-toe, black oxfords, calls his uncle “stronger than all of us.” “We do this for Connie,” says Head. He underscores Connie’s vitality, shaking his head for emphasis as he says: “He wears me out—every—day. ‘Why did they do that? Why didn’t they do this?’” This provokes smiles and chuckles from the people sitting at the circular tables decorated with trophies (known as “Wallys,” in honor of late NHRA founder Wally Parks).


Doug, holding a Wally.


Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


Doug seems quite comfortable at these sponsor events, perhaps more than his fellow drivers, Shawn Langdon and funny car driver J.R. Todd. Sponsors mean you get to do cool things, Doug explains. As he strides down Woodward Avenue on his way to Comerica Park (its title sponsor recently merged with Fifth Third), where the group will watch the Detroit Tigers take on the Houston Astros, he recounts sitting in the front row in an Elton John concert, partying with Gene Simmons in Las Vegas when KISS sponsored his dragster, and sharing a hospitality bus with Jesse James when he was dating Sandra Bullock, who once held Avery when she was a toddler.


Doug’s last name may be on each of the team’s three cars, but at the race shop or the track, his attitude is marked by humility. He gratefully defers to the expertise of Alan Johnson, whom he calls a wizard—“I’m just so fortunate that he’s actually my crew chief”—and focuses on driving the car and interacting with fans. Between sessions, he greets all comers, wandering to the metal barrier that defines the pits to sign shirts, posters, or pistons, to shake hands, and to take photographs. The intensity on display when he’s getting strapped into the race car peeks through in quiet ways, mostly in his hands. They are always moving: clasping and unclasping, fitting one set of fingers into the valleys between the knuckles, then swapping, or twiddling the black Sharpie while he sits for an interview.


This June, with fans, at the Summit Racing Equipment NHRA Nationals in Norwalk, Ohio.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Doug’s demeanor is uncommon among race car drivers, says Stewart. “If he put on somebody else’s baseball hat and he walked through the pits, nobody would even notice it was him.” Going unnoticed wouldn’t bother Doug in the least, he affirms. Doug does cut loose, on the rare race-weekend Sundays when he isn’t ferrying a plane-full of people back to Michigan. He can, confirms his marketing manager Luke Fath, ride a unicycle with a Coors Lite in each hand. One more thing, says Luke, who has vacationed with the family at their cabin in upper Michigan: “Don’t play Euchre with him.”


Doug has a deep regard for the people around him. This year’s Denso NHRA Sonoma Nationals, held July 17–19, marked 30 years since Blaine, Alan Johnson’s late brother, won his last race. On August 31, 1996, just after Blaine’s car crossed the finish line at Indianapolis Raceway Park, the engine of his dragster caught fire, exploding both tires and sending the dragster skidding into the left wall, where it tore in two and spun on its own axis down the track, into the other wall. Blaine was taken to the hospital where, after several hours of surgery, he was pronounced dead. On July 19, 2026, when Doug realized the significance of the date to Alan, he presented the trophy he had just won to his crew chief.


Cameron Neveu


Doug’s bearing changes subtly when he’s roaming Willow Run Airport in Ypsilanti, Michigan, checking in on his companies. He strides quickly through hangers and up stairs and between buildings and pausing, here and there, to explain things in his understated way. “I try to delegate myself out of as many jobs as I can so I can keep moving,” he says. He’s clearly a familiar presence; he greets people by name, and no one tenses up when he walks into a room. It makes sense: A typical workday, for him, is 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., and he’s been driving to this airport every day since the mid-‘80s.


Kalitta Air’s 747s and 777s are maintained 200 miles north at Oscoda-Wurtsmith Airport, whose 11,800 ex-military runway is far more accommodating than Willow Run’s 7543-foot one, but they, and all the other flights, are overseen at Willow Run. These days, Kalitta Air does most of its business bringing cargo from Shein and Temu over from China. When a new generation of Xbox comes out, or a new iPhone, for instance, and their manufacturers send plane loads to the U.S., they’re flown over by Kalitta Air. It also flies two 747s for UPS over the Christmas holiday rush.


The companies for which Doug is directly responsible handle shorter-range missions, including a lot of organ transplant trips, but also parts for automotive plants. His fleet of 16 737s shuttles to the automotive plants in Mexico “all the time,” he says. As strange as it may seem, the 737s compete with the semis. If anything slows down the trucks—an ice storm, for instance—the planes become the fastest way to move around freight. The companies who own the cargo bid on the internet with companies like Kalitta Charters, who are quoting all day. “It’s all about just trying to find the right-size plane,” Doug says, from a 737 freighter with its 40,000-pound payload to the fast little Learjet 45s which can carry about 3000 pounds.


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


Cameron Neveu


It’s in the maintenance shops, though, where Doug seems most at home. He’s self-effacing when we visit the sales center—though he has experience in this department, he says “these guys are a lot better at it than me”—and he clearly admires the work his mechanics do. He has special praise for the people working on the Lear 45 engine, a Honeywell TFE731-20AR: “This is our fearless team of new-gen engine mechanics, always willing to tackle anything. They all do a hell of a job.”


Cameron Neveu


For all the size and scale of the operation at Willow Run, the buildings are completely unassuming from the outside. You’d never know they contain an engine test cell, two 747 simulators, and two “brand-new” 737 simulators. Here, function trumps form. When Doug buys planes, which he typically does once or twice a year, he buys them used. Even “Connie’s baby,” the comfy Challenger business jet that is his preferred form of racetrack transportation, is no trendy statement of modern wealth: It’s filled with big, squishy seats that, compared to the slim chairs you’d find on a passenger jet, look like La-Z-Boys, complete with beige upholstery and throw blankets.


With 28 years of racing under his belt, how long will Doug stay in the NHRA? Alan Johnson admits that Doug “is no spring chicken,” but it’s clear that Johnson wouldn’t be crewing for a team whose driver wasn’t championship caliber. GM Chad Head has seen a thing or two, and he is confident that when “Dougie” feels himself slowing, he will step down of his own accord. “He ain’t slowing down any time soon,” he says with confidence.


Mitch certainly seems to be next in line. He’s been getting rides in Super Comp dragsters—“anything I can do not to own one of these things,” his dad says, with a rueful smile—and in 2026, Mitch debuted in a Top Alcohol dragster. However, it is important to Doug that his son came to racing, and airplanes, of his own accord. “He’s not some spoiled brat,” says Chad Head, who was with Mitch at a Goodyear tire test at Ohio’s Dragway 42 in July, where the younger Kalitta put on a “genuinely impressive” performance, kind of like his dad back in the day, he reflects.


Doug may be most visible on the weekends, when he’s racing, but as relentless a competitor as he is by nature, the gravitational center of his life is not the track. It’s the airport. “This is my whole life,” he says, standing on the weathered pavement of Willow Run. He isn’t still for long. After a courteous but efficient goodbye, he turns and strides into the nearest building, ready to tackle what’s next.
